title: How to Prioritize Your Book of Business Each Week
summary: Prioritising a book of business means deciding where attention can make a useful difference now.
body_markdown:
Prioritising a book of business means deciding where attention can make a useful difference now. Revenue matters, but it should not be the only input. An overdue commitment, a blocked launch, or an approaching customer decision may require action even when the account is small.


A practical system combines commitments, customer impact, timing, and available capacity. It should explain why an account is on the list and what someone is expected to do. A ranked dashboard without an action is only another thing to inspect.


## Start with obligations, not scores


Before ranking opportunities, list what the team has already promised. A commitment with an agreed date deserves attention because the customer is relying on it. If the commitment cannot be met, the next action is to communicate and revise the plan before the customer has to chase it.


Then identify customer decisions with real timing constraints. A planned rollout, procurement deadline, or executive review can create a useful window for action. Record the source of the timing rather than assuming urgency from the age of the account or the renewal month.


Finally, consider opportunities for proactive help. These matter, but they should not crowd out unresolved obligations. A team that continually starts new conversations while neglecting existing promises will struggle to build trust.


## Use a small set of explainable factors


Factor Question Example evidence


Commitment Are we already responsible for a next step? Customer-confirmed task and date


Impact What is the customer unable to do? A blocked team launch


Timing When will action become less useful? Review or decision date


Relationship change Has something material changed? New sponsor or revised objective


Readiness Can the team take a useful action now? Clear owner and available information


You can attach weights, but treat them as an operating choice rather than a validated predictive model. A simple high/medium/low assessment is often easier to challenge and maintain than a numerical score with opaque logic.


## Build the weekly review around decisions


Begin with overdue commitments and unresolved high-impact issues. For each account, ask whether the current owner and next action remain correct. Remove stale tasks and update plans that the customer has changed.


Next, inspect upcoming conversations and deadlines. The preparation task should be specific: collect the adoption evidence, confirm the support update, or prepare the stakeholder questions. “Check in” is not a sufficient action unless the reason for checking in is clear.


Then allocate remaining capacity to proactive work. Choose opportunities where the team can help the customer advance an agreed goal. Keep a visible reserve for unplanned issues rather than filling every available hour with scheduled outreach.


## A copyable prioritisation worksheet


For each account, record the customer moment, the evidence, the consequence of waiting, the next useful action, the owner, and the expected effort. Add a review date so a deferred item is not forgotten.


For example, an illustrative account has requested setup guidance before its launch. The evidence is a dated message. Waiting risks the team arriving unprepared. The action is to confirm the setup checklist and send a reviewed response. The owner estimates a short preparation task and commits to completing it before the requested date.


A different account has expressed vague interest in future expansion. The action may be to add a question to the next review, not to launch an immediate sales sequence. The worksheet makes that distinction visible.


## Protect against misleading signals


Silence is not always disengagement. A customer may be in a quiet phase or following the agreed plan without needing help. A spike in tickets may reflect healthy adoption rather than dissatisfaction. Product usage can change because of seasonality or a role transition.


Use multiple pieces of evidence before escalating an interpretation. A proposed risk should explain what changed and what information would confirm or weaken the concern. Allow account owners to correct the assessment with a reason that can be reviewed later.


The[health-score guide](https://o11.ai/blog/customer-health-score) explains how to handle incomplete and stale signals. Prioritisation should remain useful even when you do not have enough evidence for a confident risk classification.


## Make deferral an explicit decision


Not every item can be completed this week. A responsible deferral records why, when it will be reconsidered, and what change would make it urgent. It should not silently disappear from the work queue.


Separate blocked work from low-priority work. If the team cannot proceed because a customer has not confirmed a requirement, record the dependency and an appropriate follow-up point. If the work is simply less valuable than other tasks, say so internally and revisit it through the normal review.


Keep an operator override for exceptional situations. The system should allow a person to elevate an account with a reason, then evaluate whether that override was useful. A rigid score should not overrule clear customer evidence.


## Measure whether prioritisation helps


Review missed commitments, work completed, time spent preparing, and the proportion of alerts that led to a useful action. Ask whether important customer moments were overlooked. Do not judge the process only by the number of tasks created or messages sent.


If the list constantly exceeds capacity, change the service model or the definition of actionable work. Increasing alert volume will not solve a staffing or process constraint.
